items.title: Windows 11 collects data on usage of coding agents and developer tools via MissionControlAggregator.dll, reporting to Microsoft Diagnostics by default [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Windows 11 is collecting data on which coding agents and developer tools you use
items.summary:
Windows 11 includes a system component, MissionControlAggregator.dll, that tracks which coding agents like copilot.exe and developer tools such as python.exe and gcc.exe are used on the system. This data is collected by monitoring Windows events related to process activity and is saved locally before being uploaded to Microsoft Diagnostics if the user has not opted out of optional diagnostic data.

The component categorizes tools into broader groups and reports usage through Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) as bitsets indicating which tools were observed during a reporting window. It collects only presence data rather than detailed usage metrics like runtime or interaction counts. This telemetry is embedded in Windows system binaries and operates by subscribing to existing Windows process and application state events.

items.title: OpenCode launches Browse, a Chromium extension and MCP server enabling AI agents to use users' real browsers with tabs, logins, and extensions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenCode Browse
items.summary:
OpenCode has released Browse, a tool combining an MCP server and a Chromium extension that allows AI agents to operate within users' actual browsers, including Chrome, Edge, Brave, and others. The agents can open tabs in the background, interact with web pages by reading, clicking, typing, taking screenshots, and recording tabs, while handing control back to users for sensitive actions like logins, two-factor authentication, or payments.

Browse supports multiple MCP clients such as OpenCode, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Zed, and uses the user's existing logged-in sessions without requiring additional setup or keys. Users can also lend tabs to agents and restrict agents to allowed sites. Installation involves adding the Chrome extension, which guides through the setup process, with alternative command-line installation options available.

items.title: Study finds local mathematical objects and structural constraints are key for target-aligned conjecture generation from natural-language mathematical context [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Which Mathematical Context Supports Target-Aligned Conjecture Generation? A Paired Ablation Study
items.summary: Researchers conducted a paired ablation study using 61 theorems from 12 papers across four mathematical domains to determine which contextual components best support generating mathematical conjectures aligned with target theorems. They analyzed six types of context by removing or isolating each component, producing 793 conjectures to evaluate the impact on alignment with the original theorems. The study found that while components were complementary, local mathematical objects provided the strongest standalone signal, and removing structural constraints and conditions caused the largest drop in alignment. These results suggest effective conjecture generation requires combining information that identifies relevant mathematical objects with constraints that limit admissible claims.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generating mathematical conjectures from natural-language context is challenging because theorem-relevant information is distributed across multiple forms of mathematical context, including definitions, objects, assumptions, and constructions. We study which of these contextual signals help a model recover the specific claim supported by the surrounding setup, using 61 main theorems from 12 papers across four mathematical domains. For each theorem, we redact the result and represent the remaining setup using six context components. A paired ablation design compares full context, six leave-one-out conditions, and six single-component conditions, yielding 793 generated conjectures. Context components were largely complementary: removing one component usually had little effect, whereas retaining only one substantially reduced expected-theorem alignment. Local Mathematical Objects provided the strongest standalone signal, while Structural Constraints and Conditions produced the largest alignment decrease when removed. These findings suggest that target-aligned conjecture generation depends on combining information that identifies relevant objects with information that constrains admissible claims.

items.title: ReVision introduces selective intrinsic reasoning to improve tool-augmented visual question answering accuracy across six benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ReVision: Selective Intrinsic Reasoning for Tool-Augmented, Reasoning-Intensive VQA
items.summary: Researchers propose ReVision, a training-free, test-time method that allows multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to optionally reconsider visual inputs without external tools during reasoning-intensive visual question answering (VQA). Their study finds that while external tools generally improve aggregate accuracy, they can also cause answer reversals by reducing intrinsic visual reasoning. ReVision enables MLLMs to integrate intrinsic reconsideration alongside tool use, improving accuracy by 1.28% to 7.51% over standard tool use on six VQA benchmarks and outperforming the Dual-Rollout Combine method on five, with comparable reasoning-token usage.
items.description: Researchers propose ReVision, a training-free, test-time method that allows multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to optionally reconsider visual inputs without external tools during reasoning-intensive visual question answering (VQA). Their study finds that while external tools generally improve aggregate accuracy, they can also cause answer reversals by reducing intrinsic visual reasoning. ReVision enables MLLMs to integrate intrinsic reconsideration alongside tool use, improving accuracy by 1.28% to 7.51% over standard tool use on six VQA benchmarks and outperforming the Dual-Rollout Combine method on five, with comparable reasoning-token usage.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: External tools substantially expand what multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can retrieve and compute on reasoning-intensive visual questions, and aggregate accuracy typically improves when tools are available. Our empirical study across six VQA benchmarks shows that aggregate accuracy gains under tool access can coexist with answer reversals: questions answered correctly without tools but incorrectly with tools. Trajectory analysis reveals substantially shorter reasoning turns under tool access, suggesting a shift from intrinsic visual reasoning toward reliance on external outputs. We propose ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution. When invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis. The MLLM chooses if and when to use it, without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six benchmarks (1.28--7.51\%) and outperforms Dual-Rollout Combine on five, with reasoning-token use comparable to standard tool use.

items.title: Study finds probing and steering directions differ in language models, with steering favoring mean difference directions across models and layers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed three instruction-tuned language models to compare directions used for probing concepts versus steering model behavior. They found that the directions best for detecting concepts do not align with those best for steering, with steering consistently favoring directions closer to the mean difference rather than the best probe direction. This pattern held across nearly all tested layers, models, and concepts, including truthfulness and sentiment.

The study also examined transferability across models, showing that probes transferred via linear maps retained most of their probing performance, while steering effects transferred less effectively. Additionally, applying steering toward "unknown" in the PopQA dataset increased abstention rates on uncertain errors significantly more than on confident errors, though it rarely corrected errors when a correct answer was available. These findings highlight distinct roles and behaviors of probing and steering directions within and across language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19499v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator. The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.

items.title: Researchers introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law, evaluating 19 large language models across 1,860 instances [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law
items.summary: SG-LegalClarify is a new benchmark designed to test large language models (LLMs) on legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition within Singapore's unique legal system, which blends English common law with local statutes. The benchmark includes 1,100 lawyer-authored questions across 10 legal domains, featuring both fully specified and underspecified queries, with responses evaluated using lawyer-developed IRAC rubrics. Researchers assessed 19 LLMs using a multi-turn pipeline where models decide to answer or seek clarification, revealing that even the best models meet only about 70% of mandatory criteria without web search and 78% with it, and struggle to identify when clarification is needed. The team plans to release the benchmark's public split, model outputs, and evaluation tools to support further research in legal AI.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.

items.title: Researchers introduce EfficientSkill, a two-step framework that reduces token usage and improves accuracy in multi-turn LLM agents by compressing instructions and offloading reusable code [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: EfficientSkill: Learning Skills for Token-Efficient Multi-Turn Agents
items.summary: EfficientSkill addresses the problem of prompt bloat and token inflation in multi-turn large language model (LLM) agents caused by accumulating edge-case rules. The framework first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties, then prunes instructions to compress prompts, limit agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities without additional prompt cost. Evaluations on four models across benchmarks like MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench show EfficientSkill reduces output tokens by up to 80% compared to unconstrained methods while improving mean accuracy, including significant gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops. We introduce EfficientSkill, a two-step framework that first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties, and then warm-starts accuracy-guarded pruning from that skill to compress instructions, bound agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities with zero implementation prompt cost. Across four frontier, mid-tier, and open-weight models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench, EfficientSkill cuts output tokens over unconstrained EvoSkill on 11 of 12 configurations (by up to 80%) while raising mean accuracy on every benchmark, including +14.3 and +17.5 percentage-point gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast by replacing stalled loops with compact workflows. By shrinking both generated tokens and replayed history, EfficientSkill lowers total token usage and serving cost across every evaluated configuration, with or without full-prefix KV caching.

items.title: Study analyzes 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models, finding limited ablation testing and transparency in claimed novelties [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The novelty exposed: ablation, reproducibility and transparency in 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models (LLMs)
items.summary:
A 2025 analysis of 48 new large language model architectures added to the Hugging Face transformers library reveals that most reuse core components from existing models, primarily Llama. The study examines 40 randomly sampled technical reports to assess claims of novelty, ablation studies, and reproducibility disclosures, finding that only 19 of 73 novelty claims include controlled comparisons and few reports provide multiple training runs or detailed data disclosures.

The researchers also investigated whether known components were renamed to appear novel and found no evidence of hidden origins in five candidate cases. They propose seven reporting guidelines for future LLM release reports and apply them to two examples, emphasizing transparency without judging model quality or the truth of untested claims.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.20003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 2025 alone, 48 new large language model (LLM) architectures were added to the Hugging Face transformers library, and many of them arrive with a technical report that presents the model as new. What is actually new in these models, and is it tested? We put this question to LLM technical reports. We look at three things: what the reference code shows about how new open-weight architectures differ from earlier ones; what 40 randomly sampled technical reports claim as new and whether they support it with ablation studies; and what they disclose for reproducibility and transparency. In the library, 39 of the 48 architectures added in 2025 take at least two of their three core blocks from another model, most often Llama, although part of this reflects how the library writes code. In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.

items.title: Researchers evaluate decision models Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B for extracting clinical data from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports, comparing accuracy and calibration with generative models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Can decision models extract clinical data from cancer pathology reports? An evaluation of accuracy, calibration, and failure modes
items.summary:
Researchers tested two open-weight decision models, Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B, on extracting 25 clinical fields from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports against a clinical database, comparing them to generative models Qwen3.5 9B and GLM-5.3-flash. Tev1 matched Qwen3.5's accuracy at about 91.7% but was four times faster, while Nimble scored lower at 86.2%, and GLM-5.3-flash achieved 98.6%. Both decision models performed well on simple binary categories but struggled with binned measurements, unreported fields, and complex decisions like involved margins.

The study found Nimble's lower accuracy was partly due to processing 25 questions in one request, which improved when limited to two questions per request. The models' probability outputs were well calibrated overall but did not detect systematic errors within individual fields. A simulated approach of escalating uncertain answers to GLM-5.3-flash improved Tev1's accuracy to 98.2%, with 38% of answers escalated. The authors suggest decision models can efficiently extract explicit findings from pathology reports on local hardware but recommend validating them for specific use cases, restricting to reliable fields, and combining with other methods for numeric data extraction.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.20129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decision models are a new class of language model that, instead of generating text, choose one option per question from a fixed list and return a probability for every option. They have not yet been evaluated on clinical text. We evaluated two open-weights decision models, Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B, for extracting 25 fields from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports from a single centre, against a prospectively maintained clinical database. We compared them with two generative models: Qwen3.5 9B, run locally, and GLM-5.3-flash, run through a cloud API. Tev1 reached a mean field accuracy of 0.917 (95% CI 0.913 to 0.920), the same as Qwen3.5 9B (0.918; p = 0.26), and was four times faster (15 s against 61 s per report). Nimble reached 0.862 and GLM-5.3-flash 0.986. Both decision models matched GLM-5.3-flash on simple dichotomous categories. They were weak on measurements binned into categories, on fields whose correct answer was not reported, and on some complex decisions (e.g. involved margins). We found that the main cause of the inferior performance of Nimble's came from asking 25 questions in one request: with two questions per request, its accuracy improved. Pooled over fields, the returned probabilities were well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.022 and 0.026), but they did not flag systematic errors within single fields. A simulated strategy of sending answers with a probability below 0.94 to GLM-5.3-flash raised Tev1's accuracy to 0.982, with 38% of answers escalated. Decision models can extract explicitly stated findings from pathology reports quickly on local hardware and return useful probabilities. They should be validated in the configuration in which they will be used, restricted to the fields in which they are reliable, and combined with other methods for numeric values.

items.title: Researchers propose deterministic validation gates for large language model-driven vibration testing of LEO constellation satellites, achieving near-perfect accuracy and error detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps
items.summary:
Researchers developed a method using deterministic validation gates to ensure accuracy in engineering analysis driven by large language models (LLMs), applied to sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites. Their approach uses multiple checks including unit consistency, physical plausibility, and agreement between independent models to prevent errors and hallucinations in data extracted from Chinese test records by LLMs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus.

The system extracted configurations with 76 fields, achieving fact-level F1 scores between 0.98 and 1.0 across variants, and successfully detected all real and injected errors that would have otherwise gone unnoticed. Retraining models on LLM-generated datasets reproduced results within GPU nondeterminism. The study also found that direct LLM curve forecasting performed no better than linear extrapolation, while a small physics-structured network significantly improved prediction accuracy, indicating when trained models should replace direct LLM predictions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.20579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly drive engineering analysis end to end, turning textual records into the inputs of numerical programs, but a plausible and wrong value can pass silently into a decision. We propose deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, a general paradigm in which a typed configuration produced by LLMs is consumed only after it passes deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, agreement between independent models, consistency with measurement exports and the applicability of trained models. The gates target hallucinations from two directions, since quote checking catches fabricated content while agreement between models catches errors of omission that quote checking misses. We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. Fact-level F1 ranged from 0.98 to 1.0 on five input variants, with all repairs frozen on development inputs and evaluated on held-out inputs. With all gates, 20 of 20 configurations produced notching results bit for bit identical to the gold run, and all 17 real and injected errors in consumed fields were stopped, of which 16 would have run without gates. Retraining the bound model on a dataset built from an LLM configuration reproduced its results within GPU nondeterminism. We also report a negative result of practical value. Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.

items.title: Researchers propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection for safety-preserving fine-tuning of medical large language models, improving safety rates by up to 4.64 points while maintaining medical capability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Safety-Preserving Medical LLM Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Data Selection
items.summary: Researchers introduce Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) to enhance safety in supervised fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) for patient-facing medical applications. S-BDS ranks training samples to improve medical knowledge while controlling risks, combining clinician-validated safe data with unscreened medical instruction data. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models show S-BDS achieves higher safety rates than existing methods on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench benchmarks, with a trade-off between medical capability and safety adjustable via training parameters.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.20643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As general large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted for patient-facing medical applications, improving medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks remains a critical challenge. Large-scale medical instruction data are essential for acquiring domain knowledge through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but unsafe responses can undermine existing safety alignment. To address this problem, we propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) for safety-preserving medical SFT. By controlling selection-weight concentration, S-BDS enables reliable sample ranking over large candidate pools and identifies training examples that improve medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks. We combine clinician-validated safe data and selected data with unscreened medical instruction data for SFT, and jointly evaluate medical capability and patient-facing safety on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench, respectively. Experiments across Llama and Qwen models show that S-BDS achieves the highest safe rates among all compared methods, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.64 and 3.00 percentage points, respectively, while maintaining competitive medical capability. Further experiments show that varying the safety-oriented weight during SFT controls the trade-off between medical capability and patient-facing safety.

items.title: Nemotron releases 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open small language model optimized for speed and accuracy in fast conversational agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
items.summary: Nemotron has introduced the 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, a small language model derived from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for efficient memory use and speed in conversational AI applications. The model enhances multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding, targeting local voice assistants, interactive personas, and embedded or edge devices running on platforms like GeForce RTX and Jetson. It achieves the highest average accuracy and generates fewer output tokens compared to its predecessors and competitors across 21 benchmarks. The release includes a DFlash drafter that significantly improves decode speed and generation throughput over previous models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.20771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

items.title: Researchers identify Experience Rot where AI agents fail after silent tool changes, with novices outperforming experienced agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
items.summary: Researchers demonstrate that AI agents relying on accumulated experience fail most tasks after silent changes to their tools, a phenomenon they term Experience Rot. In tests using the Model Context Protocol, experienced agents reused outdated calls without verifying updated interfaces, leading to incorrect success reports, while novice agents adapted more successfully. This failure occurs across various memory types and worsens with more experience. Attempts to mitigate the issue through update announcements or directing agents to documentation were largely ineffective when documentation was incomplete.
items.description: Researchers demonstrate that AI agents relying on accumulated experience fail most tasks after silent changes to their tools, a phenomenon they term Experience Rot. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.20922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.

items.title: Researchers introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark using world distillation for device control evaluation across Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes and 1,166 functions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking
items.summary:
SynthDCB is a new benchmark designed to scale device-control evaluation by creating interactive worlds through world distillation, which modularizes device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects. It supports multiple domains including Home, Car, and Phone, encompassing 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, and enables task validation and agent evaluation via state correctness and tool-call traces.

The benchmark includes five task families with 32 subtypes and was tested on 2,560 tasks across seven models, with the best model achieving a 68.2% Pass@1 score. Analysis identified challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. SynthDCB also demonstrates improved token efficiency and scalability compared to Codex, reducing token consumption significantly while covering broader capabilities, establishing executable world construction as a foundation for scalable device-control benchmarking and verifiable agent evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both the worlds agents interact with and the tasks they must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation. World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components, which are composed into interactive worlds with explicit states, actions, and temporal dynamics. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis, allowing new capabilities to enter evaluation through a shared construction pipeline. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. The stateful design enables task validation and agent evaluation through state correctness and tool-call traces. We evaluate seven models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 68.2% Pass@1. Error analysis reveals challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. Construction experiments demonstrate scalability across domains and token efficiency: world distillation reduces token consumption by 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% relative to Codex with low and xhigh reasoning effort, respectively, while achieving broader capability coverage. SynthDCB makes executable world construction the basis of scalable device-control benchmarking, connecting an expanding space of capabilities and interactions to verifiable agent evaluation.

items.title: Researchers propose Distributional On-Policy Distillation to improve offline on-policy distillation efficiency and student-teacher alignment in multi-turn agentic search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rethinking Offline On-Policy Distillation: From Scalar Advantages to Distributional Supervision
items.summary:
On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher model capabilities through token-level feedback but is computationally expensive due to repeated teacher evaluations. Offline methods like Lightning OPD reduce this cost by caching teacher log-probabilities on fixed rollouts but underperform compared to supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in multi-turn agentic search setups. Researchers identify teacher-reference mismatches and distributional flattening as key issues with scalar advantage supervision on fixed rollouts, leading to suboptimal student outputs.

To address these challenges, the team proposes Distributional On-Policy Distillation (DistOPD), an offline method that retains candidate-token probabilities from both reference and teacher models at selected positions while aggregating remaining tokens into a residual category. DistOPD achieves performance comparable to online OPD, improves alignment between student and teacher models, and requires similar GPU training time as Lightning OPD, offering a more effective and efficient approach for offline distillation in agentic search contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher capabilities through token-level feedback on student-generated trajectories, but repeatedly evaluating fresh rollouts with the teacher is computationally expensive. Offline methods such as Lightning OPD reduce this cost by caching recorded tokens' teacher log-probabilities on fixed reference rollouts. By extending the idea to a multi-turn agentic search setup, we find that it consistently underperforms the SFT starting point trained by the same teacher. We empirically observe greater teacher--reference mismatch than in mathematical reasoning and post-training distributional flattening, and theoretically show that scalar advantage supervision on fixed rollouts admits solutions with flattened output distributions under suitable conditions. Motivated by these findings, we propose Distributional On-Policy Distillation (DistOPD), a simple yet effective offline OPD method that retains candidate-token probabilities from both reference and teacher at selected positions and aggregates the remaining parts into a residual token. On agentic search, DistOPD achieves performance comparable to online OPD while improving student--teacher alignment and using training GPU-hours comparable to Lightning OPD.

items.title: Study finds hard-negative fine-tuning improves spatial reasoning in multimodal large language models with mixed effects across model families and question types [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Does Hard-Negative Fine-Tuning Teach Multimodal Large Language Models? Controlled Evidence from a Compositional Benchmark
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated the impact of hard-negative fine-tuning on three multimodal large language model families using CompHall, a compositional benchmark with 2,860 forced-choice questions covering spatial, attribute, counting, and part-whole reasoning. They found that fine-tuning improved spatial-relation question accuracy in all models when using a corrected loss function, but gains were limited or inconsistent across other question types and models. The study also revealed that some questions could be answered from text alone, indicating that compositional failures do not necessarily cause hallucinations in these models.

The analysis included controls such as gray-image evaluation, multiple random seeds, option-order tests, and independent benchmarks to ensure robustness. Results showed that the original fine-tuning method harmed some models by focusing on image-placeholder tokens, while the corrected approach required spatial training questions to achieve improvements. Additionally, fine-tuning increased a yes-bias in one model variant, and gains did not generalize broadly across all question types or models tested.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18701v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fine-tuning on hard negatives is a popular way to improve the compositional reasoning of vision-language models, but when accuracy goes up it is rarely clear what the model actually learned. We ask this question for multimodal large language models. We use CompHall, 2,860 forced-choice questions (spatial, attribute, counting and part-whole) with two graded hard negatives each, three model families (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT and Idefics2), and controls that such studies often lack: gray-image evaluation, three seeds, option-order tests, control arms trained on different question types, and independent benchmarks. We find four things. First, CompHall is not a pure test of vision: part-whole questions can be answered from the text alone (66-95% without the image), and per-image accuracy is unrelated to an object-hallucination probe (r = -0.05), so we see no evidence that compositional failures drive hallucination. Second, the original fine-tuning method scored mostly image-placeholder tokens and hurt both LLaVA models. With a corrected loss, fine-tuning raises accuracy on the spatial-relation questions of CV-Bench in all three families, by +3.2, +23.1 and +6.0 points (averaged over both option orders). Control arms show that the gain needs spatial training questions, and for LLaVA-NeXT about two-thirds of it appears even on relation words that were only wrong options in training. Third, the gain is not general: on CompHall itself it is significant only for LLaVA-NeXT (+6.9 points) and not detectable for Idefics2, it reaches about 3 points at most on true/false statements, and LLaVA-1.5 fine-tuned on other question types learns to answer "true" too often. Fourth, both losses raise the yes-bias of LLaVA-1.5 on POPE.

items.title: Researchers analyze large language models' internal oncology representations, showing they generate consistent cancer patient profiles and predict 12-month survival with up to 89.9% accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Large language models as oncology world models
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated large language models (LLMs) for their internal representation of oncology by generating synthetic cancer patient cases based on tumor type. They found that LLMs produce similar patient profiles within cancer types and follow biomarker and treatment logic in most clinical scenarios. The models predicted 12-month survival rates with higher accuracy than observed in real patients when continuing patient trajectories.

The team developed the Clinical State Space framework to dynamically represent patient trajectories, applying it to both synthetic and real patients. While the study identified limitations in current LLM world models, it suggests that improved models could support digital twin applications in oncology, with the framework providing a method to evaluate such models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize cancer patient cases, but their internal representation of oncology, or world model, has not been explored systematically. By only specifying tumor type, we show that LLMs tend to generate similar patients per cancer, with on average 81.0% to 93.2% of a cancer's patients sharing the most frequent value of each baseline feature. By systematically varying patient features in 12 clinical scenarios, we show that they follow biomarker and treatment logic in 29 of 36 model-scenario assessments, against 1 of 12 when previous treatment or frailty matters. Continuing real patient trajectories, an LLM predicted 89.9% 12-month survival, and 79.2% with similar patients as examples, against 72.2% observed. To represent these trajectories, we developed the Clinical State Space, a dynamic representation framework that we also applied to real patients. Despite the limits we show, improved world models may support digital twins, which our framework can evaluate.

items.title: Nahual introduces a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for combined text and 3D molecular sequences, outperforming specialized models on twelve chemistry tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms
items.summary: Nahual is a new generative model that integrates language and 3D molecular data using a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion approach. It employs next-token diffusion to handle continuous 3D coordinates within a causal transformer framework, enabling expressive autoregression without increasing context size. The model is trained end-to-end on twelve diverse 3D chemistry tasks, including microsolvation, molecular conformer search, and adsorption on metal surfaces, surpassing state-of-the-art specialized models in crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. This work demonstrates the potential for scaling generalist decoder-only models to achieve native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry domains. The code for Nahual is publicly available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/nahual.

items.originalTitle: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
items.summary:
Researchers introduce staged semantic distillation, a method that preserves non-structured semantics in a low-compute non-LLM student model trained from one recorded trace of a staged LLM agent used in market simulation. The approach uses a frozen encoder to map teacher outputs to vectors, enabling the student to train efficiently with scheduled self-history and stage-specific visibility, achieving close alignment with the teacher's decisions while running without language model calls or text generation.

The method was tested on a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator trace, producing a 13.2 million-parameter deterministic student that trains in under 30 minutes on a single 8-GB GPU and runs decisions in 0.14 milliseconds each. The surrogate model maintains semantic channels effectively, reaching balanced accuracy above 0.83 on teacher-forced replay and showing gains over no-semantic retraining. The study highlights the importance of deployment scheduling and content handling in training, offering a faster alternative to running the original large language model agent for simulation tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.

items.title: Researchers propose a two-regime framework to evaluate large language model agent markets by separating information simulation and macro emergence using macro-level observations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a framework that organizes large language model (LLM) agents into multi-agent markets acting as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics. The framework separates model capability into two stages: information simulation, translating macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, translating micro behavior to macro outcomes, which cannot be captured by a single aggregate score. They propose a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path daily without altering individual agent decisions and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone.

The framework includes a reference-only regime measuring realization and structural bias through symmetric true and flipped references, and an information-injection regime where external information dilutes the reference, leaving only the true-flipped gap interpretable. Experiments on five single-index LLM-agent markets show that announcing a target path shifts realized paths toward the target under both regimes and information conditions, with improved tracking scores relative to no-reference paths. Structural bias and realization metrics vary with technical and fundamental data shares, demonstrating the framework's ability to assess model capabilities using observable macro-level scores.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs. This paper separates a model's capability into two stages that a single aggregate score cannot separate: information simulation, from macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, from micro behavior to the macro outcome. We introduce a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path day by day without touching individual decisions, orders, or matching, and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. In the reference-only regime the symmetric true and flipped references share a common level R, which measures realization under the announced reference, while their paired gap B measures structural bias; in the information-injection regime external information dilutes the reference, so only the true-flipped gap Delta remains interpretable. On five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target path shifts the realized path toward the announced target on both announced references under both information conditions. Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.

items.title: Researchers find pretraining optimizer gains do not consistently transfer to KL distillation in language models across multiple optimizer comparisons [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
items.summary:
A study compares matrix-structured optimizers like SOAP and Shampoo reductions with elementwise optimizers AdamW and AdaGrad during KL distillation of language models initialized from instruction-tuned checkpoints. The results show that none of the matrix-structured optimizers consistently outperform AdamW or AdaGrad in terms of validation KL or training time across four Qwen student-teacher model pairs under a fixed training budget. AdamW generally achieves the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be faster at larger scales, and matrix-structured methods incur overhead or inconsistent performance depending on the recipe and model pair.

These findings suggest that optimizer improvements observed during language model pretraining do not automatically apply to short-horizon KL distillation tasks and should be re-evaluated for the specific distillation objective and system constraints. The study highlights the need to tailor optimizer choices to the target training regime rather than assuming gains transfer from pretraining to distillation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19419v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality versus trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.

items.title: Researchers evaluate MAGIC influence-function method for trajectory data attribution on GPT-2-style models, finding reliable predictions in short checkpoint windows but poor correlation over full runs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MathaMAGICal: Validating Trajectory Data Attribution During Capability Acquisition
items.summary:
Researchers tested the MAGIC method for trajectory data attribution on 86M- and 152M-parameter GPT-2-style models trained on multistep arithmetic tasks using filtered web text and synthetic math data. They found that full-run attribution at 86M parameters suffered from numerical overflow and low correlation with retraining results, while short checkpoint windows produced stable and accurate predictions at both model scales. Individual training block rankings predicted retraining outcomes only within the same run and did not generalize across different seeds or hyperparameters, but format-level patterns were consistent across runs.

The study also identified two data families—worked examples and primitive facts—that were overrepresented in both the most helpful and harmful score tails, indicating strong local sensitivity distinct from overall net benefit. These findings suggest that trajectory attribution methods like MAGIC are reliable within validated short windows and can provide insights that generalize across training runs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Influence-function-based methods like MAGIC provide exact first-order scores for trajectory data attribution, yet only retraining indicates whether those scores accurately predict data removal. We evaluate MAGIC on $86$M- and $152$M-parameter GPT-2-style models learning multistep arithmetic from scratch on filtered web text and four synthetic math families. Full-run attribution at $86$M suffers from numerical overflow, and even with metagradient clipping, scores correlate near chance with retraining (linear datamodeling score, LDS, $0.17$--$0.22$). In contrast, short checkpoint windows yield stable, accurate predictions at both scales (LDS $0.86$--$0.99$ across four $100$-step windows at $152$M), whereas a single-checkpoint gradient-dot baseline shows near-zero correlation. Rankings of individual training blocks predict retraining only within that single run and do not transfer across seeds or hyperparameters ($\rho \le 0.09$), whereas format-level patterns replicate across runs. Two data families, worked examples and primitive facts, occupy $2.1$--$2.6\times$ their corpus share in both the helpful and harmful $5\%$ score tails, reflecting strong bidirectional local sensitivity distinct from net benefit under multi-epoch family deletion. These results show that trajectory attribution is reliable within short, validated windows and yields family-level insights that generalize across runs.

items.title: Researchers propose using training-data attribution to guide pretraining data curation by identifying testable data properties for reusable selection criteria [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Data Attribution Should Steer Pretraining
items.summary:
Researchers argue that pretraining data curation should be guided by training-data attribution, which identifies testable data properties that can serve as reusable criteria for selecting training documents. This approach contrasts with influence-driven selectors that rank documents for a single run, as attributed data properties can be evaluated across different corpora and model checkpoints to better measure usefulness.

The paper specifies a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, tests candidate data changes, and defines evidence requirements for various claim types related to data value. The authors also present a falsifiable comparison of their method against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal computational cost, aiming to improve pretraining efficiency and effectiveness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pretraining data curation decides what a model learns from, yet what makes a document worth learning from depends on what the model already knows. Influence-driven selectors already rank documents to improve one run; we argue that training-data attribution should steer pretraining by identifying testable data properties that become reusable curation criteria, evaluated on new data against cheaper selectors at matched total cost, discovery included. A document ranking is consumed by the run it was computed for, whereas an explained data property can be tested across corpora and checkpoints, especially where familiar quality signals diverge from measured usefulness. Because historical contribution, an understandable explanation, and future data value require distinct evidence, we specify a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, tests candidate data changes, and states for five claim types what evidence each requires and what none establishes. We close with a falsifiable comparison against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal total compute.

items.title: Researchers compare in-context learning, reinforcement learning, and self-distillation for test-time adaptation of LLM agents across multiple environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Should LLM Agents Adapt at Test Time? In Context, in Weights, or Both
items.summary: Researchers evaluated 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline using Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments to determine how large language model (LLM) agents should adapt at test time—through in-context learning (ICL), weight updates via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (GRPO), self-distillation (SDPO), or combinations thereof. They found that ICL alone provided the largest improvement in mean success rate, increasing it from 28.8% to 49.4%, while adding GRPO further raised success to 51.6%. SDPO showed mixed effects. Analysis revealed that ICL reduced environment lookups and attempt lengths but often skipped task inspection and verification, behaviors that GRPO helped restore without increasing lookups. These results suggest that combining context retention and weight updates can enhance LLM agent adaptation by refining how retained experience is used.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.

items.title: Researchers evaluate large language models on choosing future research directions, finding 45% to 67.5% alignment with human authors across 80 comparisons from 19 ML papers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Eliciting Research Taste in LLMs through Future Research Direction Choice
items.summary:
Researchers studied how large language models (LLMs) exhibit research taste by evaluating their ability to choose future research directions given a research goal and current results. They compared eight LLMs against human-authored future-work directions from 19 machine learning papers published between December 2025 and February 2026, measuring alignment, stable divergence, and unstable choice as behavioral indicators.

The evaluation involved 80 pairwise comparisons presenting a research goal, hypotheses, key results, and two candidate future directions—one recommended by the paper's author and one plausible distractor. Author alignment among LLMs ranged from 45.0% to 67.5%, with stable divergence between 15.0% and 36.2%. These divergences persisted under various controls, and some non-author preferences were shared across models. The study identified common model preferences toward scaling, generalization, and trade-offs between methodological and infrastructure extensions.

This work serves as an early descriptive evaluation of research taste profiles in LLMs and aims to inform understanding and steering of their research preferences as they take on more autonomous roles in open-ended scientific discovery.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Research taste is increasingly discussed in the context of AI scientists, yet remains little studied or measured in LLMs. This judgment matters especially in open-ended research, where a direction must be chosen before a verifiable objective is available. We operationalize research taste through one task of the scientific workflow: choosing which future research direction to pursue given a research goal and current results. Rather than predicting downstream scientometric metrics or treating author choices as objectively correct, we evaluate models against human-authored future-work directions and report author alignment, stable divergence, and unstable choice as behavioral measures of research-direction preference. We construct an order-controlled evaluation of 80 pairwise comparisons from 19 ML papers published between December 2025 and February 2026 across four subdomains. Each query presents a research goal, hypotheses tested with key results, and two candidate future directions: one author-recommended direction and one plausible distractor sampled from a similar paper. Across eight LLMs, author alignment ranges from 45.0% to 67.5%, while stable divergence ranges from 15.0% to 36.2%. These divergences largely persist under similarity controls, prompt ablations, and an author-preference framing check, and inter-model agreement suggests that some non-author preferences are shared across models. We characterize what models diverge toward using transition-category labels and selected reasoning examples, finding recurring movement toward scaling/generalization and trade-offs between methodological and infrastructure/data extensions. We view this as an early descriptive evaluation for eliciting research taste profiles in LLMs, and as a step toward understanding and steering their research preferences as they take on more autonomous roles in novel open-ended scientific discovery.

items.title: Researchers propose Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (TA-OPSD) to improve language model reasoning by addressing premature stopping and repetition in generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning When to Continue and When to Stop: Termination-Aware OPSD
items.summary: Researchers identify a termination mismatch in On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) where language models either stop reasoning too early or generate repetitive, unproductive outputs. They propose TA-OPSD, which adds two objectives to align teacher and student models on when to continue or stop reasoning and to reduce repetitive generation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 models (1.7B/4B/8B parameters) show TA-OPSD outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all scales. Ablation studies confirm the new objectives effectively reduce premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation, improving overall termination behavior in language model reasoning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.19925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves language model reasoning by distilling from a frozen teacher initialized identically to the student and conditioned on privileged information. However, we identify an underexplored termination mismatch in OPSD: the student fails to reliably learn when to continue and when to stop. This mismatch manifests in two opposing failure modes-premature termination, where reasoning stops before sufficient progress is made, and repetition-driven over-generation, where the model continues generating after reasoning has stalled. Our analysis shows that the teacher-student discrepancy on EOS grows during OPSD training, while length-capped trajectories are frequently dominated by unproductive repetition. To address this issue, we propose TA-OPSD (Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation), which augments the original OPSD objective with two targeted objectives. Stop/Continue Distillation addresses premature termination by explicitly aligning the teacher and student on whether reasoning should continue, while Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training addresses repetition-driven over-generation by discouraging repetitive continuations in the student's failed trajectories. The resulting objective improves termination behavior from complementary directions: continuing when further reasoning is needed and stopping when reasoning becomes unproductive. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 (1.7B/4B/8B) show that TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all three model scales. Beyond the performance gains, ablation and behavioral analyses show that the two proposed objectives effectively mitigate their corresponding termination failures, reducing both premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation.

items.title: Researchers develop LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation framework to estimate outpatient visit prices from hospital price transparency data, improving accuracy across three Maryland hospitals [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Estimating Outpatient Visit Prices from Hospital Price Transparency Data using Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers developed a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework using large language models (LLMs) to estimate outpatient visit prices from hospital price transparency data at three major hospitals in Maryland. The GPT-BM25 hybrid retriever outperformed other methods, reducing mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) to 19.44% for individual procedures and 4.90% for procedure groups compared to much higher errors in baseline models. The approach also showed promise in symptom-based visit cost estimation through synthetic simulations.

The study highlights challenges such as heterogeneous data formats, duplicate entries, and limited insurer-negotiated rate availability that affect price estimation accuracy. Despite these issues, the framework substantially improved cost estimates over no-RAG baselines, suggesting that LLMs integrating price transparency data could help patients access more accurate healthcare cost information.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.20261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective: Hospital care prices in the United States have increased substantially, yet patients lack effective tools to access and compare costs. We aimed to develop and evaluate an LLM-based approach for improving access to and use of hospital price transparency (PT) data. Materials and Methods: To estimate visit prices, we used a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework to analyze PT files from three major hospitals in Maryland and the surrounding region. We compared BM25, OpenAI embedding models, and a GPT-BM25 hybrid against a no-RAG baseline for cost estimation of individual procedures and procedure groups, then evaluated the best approach for symptom-based visit cost estimation using synthetic simulations. Results: Across hospitals, the GPT-BM25 retriever achieved the best performance, with average price MAPE of 19.44% for individual procedures and 4.90% for groups, compared with 147.98% and 82.82%, respectively, for the no-RAG baseline. In simulations, our framework correctly identified approximately 50% of reference procedures and reduced MAPE relative to the LLM-only baseline at two of the three hospitals, while achieving comparable performance at the third. Discussion: Our framework uses RAG to improve care price estimation in real-world settings. Compared with the no-RAG baseline, it substantially improved cost estimates for both individual procedures and procedure groups. Improvements were smaller in synthetic simulations, likely because inferring procedures from clinical information is more complex. Practical challenges remain, including heterogeneous PT file formats, unexplained duplicate entries, and limited availability of insurer-negotiated rates. Conclusion: LLMs that effectively integrate PT data show strong potential to provide patients with more accessible and accurate healthcare cost estimates.

items.title: Researchers propose ConvRSI framework for parallel multi-agent self-improvement using convolution, improving performance by 5% and reducing inference cost and latency on MATH-500 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Recursion to Convolution: Parallel Self-Improvement for Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary:
Researchers introduce ConvRSI, a framework that parallelizes multi-agent self-improvement by combining intra-agent convolution to refine related features and inter-agent graph convolution to aggregate messages based on collaboration topology. This approach operates in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeated decoding and re-encoding, addressing challenges of sequential dependencies and high computational costs in multi-agent systems.

Experiments on the MATH-500 dataset show that ConvRSI achieves a 5.04% performance improvement while reducing inference cost by 17.27% and latency by 45.11% compared to RecursiveMAS. The framework also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing topologies as adjacency matrices, demonstrating the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. The researchers have made their code and datasets publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.20891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in https://github.com/LYA2333/ConvRSI.

items.title: Researchers test four methods of using embedding-map distances to guide large language model ideation against subsequent developments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next
items.summary:
A study evaluates whether selecting points far from existing work in embedding maps can effectively guide ideation in large language models (LLMs). Four tests compare these distance-based approaches against actual later outputs in text, games, patents, and academic papers to assess their predictive and generative value.

The tests reveal that random distant points rarely correspond to meaningful text, and LLM-generated continuations tend to stay closer to source material than actual citing papers. Density-based gap scores show limited ability to forecast growth in content areas, and no clear pattern emerges linking distance to inspiration quality. The study uses data from sources including arXiv papers, Steam games, and patents, with results registered before and after analysis to ensure rigor.

These findings suggest that embedding-map distances alone may not reliably guide creative ideation or predict future developments, highlighting the complexity of innovation processes and the limitations of current embedding-based heuristics for generating novel ideas.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.21408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.

items.title: Researchers analyze what small language models learn from an exact verifier in authorization policy explanations, achieving up to 92% accuracy on trained policies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
items.summary: Researchers studied how small language models learn to explain authorization policy decisions when provided with an exact verifier that identifies minimal sufficient reasons for blocking tool calls. The models receive one request and decision, with multiple opportunities to query altered requests and sufficiency of fact sets, enabling evaluation against ground truth rather than proxies. A fine-tuned 4B parameter model reached 92% accuracy on the policy it was trained on, outperforming frontier models that found exact reasons about half the time. The study found that models trained with algorithmic teaching learned fixed schedules of sufficiency checks, which did not generalize well to unseen policies, while prompting improved minimality in explanations. Reinforcement learning with exact rewards did not improve held-out accuracy but shifted the model's strategy toward sufficiency checks rather than policy probing. The findings clarify how exact verifiers affect training but do not necessarily enhance overall model performance.
