items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.21529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate reward hacking in reinforcement learning using exact process oracles over 124,416 contexts, revealing vulnerabilities in optimistic verifiers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
items.summary:
Researchers built a setting where true rewards are exactly computable via executable authorization policies across 124,416 contexts, allowing an oracle to list minimal sufficient reasons for decisions. They degraded verifiers along seven realistic axes and trained models against each while scoring rollouts with the exact verifier, identifying four distinct verifier phenotypes including optimistic verifiers vulnerable to reward padding hacks.

The study found that optimistic verifiers showed decreased true faithfulness despite high proxy sufficiency, while outcome-only verifiers saturated and stopped teaching. The researchers conducted nine configurations across multiple frameworks, model vendors, and settings, observing consistent phenotypes and positive sufficiency damage in most replications. They released the testbed, training tools, and 14 real public policies ported to executable oracles to support further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.21538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

items.title: Researchers introduce Latent Lattice language models that add persistent per-layer horizontal latent streams to improve Transformer performance, reducing perplexity on 20B-token datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Latent Lattice Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers propose Latent Lattice language models that increase computational capacity by maintaining persistent per-layer horizontal latent streams alongside the vertical residual stream in Transformers. This approach enhances attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding, leading to lower validation perplexity compared to parameter-matched baseline Transformers. Experiments on models trained with 20 billion FineWeb-Edu tokens show a reduction in perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 for a 406M-parameter Lattice model, with further improvements when combined with other residual-stream enhancements.

The Lattice method also improves performance across various architectural variants including Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and hybrids, outperforming baselines even with smaller native state sizes. These results suggest that adding persistent per-layer states offers a complementary axis for scaling language model computation beyond increasing depth or looped layers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.21608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.

items.title: Researchers present a unified framework for controlling large language models, analyzing preference-utility trade-offs and introducing SPLIT steering to improve control while preserving output quality [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Steering Works: Toward a Unified View of Language Model Parameter Dynamics
items.summary: Researchers propose a unified view of methods for controlling large language models (LLMs), such as local weight fine-tuning, LoRA adaptation, and activation-based interventions, framing them as dynamic weight updates driven by control signals. They introduce a preference-utility analysis that measures the tendency toward target concepts (preference) and coherent, task-valid generation (utility) on a shared scale, revealing a consistent trade-off where stronger control increases preference but reduces utility. The study explains this trade-off through an activation manifold perspective, where control shifts representations toward target concepts but can push them off the model's valid-generation manifold, reducing utility. Based on this analysis, the researchers develop a new steering method called SPLIT that enhances preference while better maintaining utility, with code made publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.02343v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Methods for controlling large language models (LLMs), including local weight fine-tuning, LoRA-based adaptation, and activation-based interventions, are often studied in isolation, obscuring their connections and making comparison difficult. In this work, we present a unified view that frames these interventions as dynamic weight updates induced by a control signal, placing them within a single conceptual framework. Building on this view, we propose a unified preference-utility analysis that separates control effects into preference, defined as the tendency toward a target concept, and utility, defined as coherent and task-valid generation, and measures both on a shared log-odds scale using polarity-paired contrastive examples. Across methods, we observe a consistent trade-off between preference and utility: stronger control increases preference while predictably reducing utility. We further explain this behavior through an activation manifold perspective, in which control shifts representations along target-concept directions to enhance preference, while utility declines primarily when interventions push representations off the model's valid-generation manifold. Finally, we introduce a new steering approach SPLIT guided by this analysis that improves preference while better preserving utility. Code is available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit/blob/main/examples/SPLIT.md.

items.originalTitle: How Controllable Are Large Language Models? A Unified Evaluation across Behavioral Granularities
items.summary: Researchers have developed SteerEval, a hierarchical benchmark designed to assess the controllability of large language models (LLMs) in socially sensitive contexts by evaluating language features, sentiment, and personality across three specification levels. The benchmark connects high-level behavioral intent to specific textual outputs and reveals that control tends to weaken at finer-grained levels. SteerEval provides a structured and interpretable framework to guide safer and more controllable LLM behavior, aiming to support future research in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.02578v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially sensitive domains, yet their unpredictable behaviors, ranging from misaligned intent to inconsistent personality, pose significant risks. We introduce SteerEval, a hierarchical benchmark for evaluating LLM controllability across three domains: language features, sentiment, and personality. Each domain is structured into three specification levels: L1 (what to express), L2 (how to express), and L3 (how to instantiate), connecting high-level behavioral intent to concrete textual output. Using SteerEval, we systematically evaluate contemporary steering methods, revealing that control often degrades at finer-grained levels. Our benchmark offers a principled and interpretable framework for safe and controllable LLM behavior, serving as a foundation for future research.

items.title: Researchers release Metacognitive Profile Atlas analyzing confidence discrimination across 33 leading LLMs on 1,500 MMLU items by domain [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Metacognitive Profile Atlas: Domain-level confidence discrimination in 33 frontier LLMs on MMLU
items.summary:
The Metacognitive Profile Atlas provides answer and verbalized confidence data from 33 advanced large language models (LLMs) tested on 1,500 MMLU items grouped into six subject domains. The study finds that confidence best discriminates correct from incorrect answers in Applied/Professional domains and least effectively in Formal Reasoning and Natural Science, with statistical significance across the population of models. Individual model profiles show low reliability, though some within-family similarities are noted, particularly for Anthropic models.
The dataset includes 46,157 scored observations after excluding parser-imputed values and distinguishes genuine monitoring improvements from error removal in model versions. The analysis also reveals that some models perform better with verbalized confidence than with binary-probe confidence measures. This version incorporates peer review revisions and corrects earlier data artifacts, providing a resource for further exploration of metacognitive abilities in frontier LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.06673v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We release the Metacognitive Profile Atlas, a corpus of answer-plus-verbalized-confidence data from 33 frontier LLMs on 1,500 MMLU items stratified into six subject-group bins (46,157 scored observations after excluding parser-supplied values). The data allow Type-2 AUROC, the degree to which confidence discriminates correct from incorrect answers, to be decomposed by domain. The reliable finding is a population-level ordering on MMLU. Confidence discriminates best on Applied/Professional items (mean AUROC .750; ranked first in 100% of bootstrap resamples) and worst on Formal Reasoning and Natural Science (bottom two in 93% and 92%; Friedman chi^2(5) = 28.26, p < .0001). After Holm correction Applied exceeds Formal, Science, Social and Humanities; no other pair survives, including Applied versus Factual. The ordering holds when imprecise cells are excluded or down-weighted. Per-model six-domain profiles are not reliable (median split-half r = .16) and are released for exploration only; the six bins are a pragmatic grouping, not a latent construct. Within-family similarity of profile shape is significant overall, but after multiplicity correction only Anthropic is individually supported. Paired-item analysis separates genuine monitoring gains (Opus 4.1 to 4.5 and 4.7) from error removal (Gemma 3 27B to Gemma 4 31B). Models whose binary-probe confidence failed or could not be certified on a separate battery discriminate well under verbalized confidence, and three Gemma 3 models show the reverse pattern. This version incorporates revisions committed during peer review, corrects descriptions of external validity-screen results, and excludes 980 parser-imputed confidence values for GPT-oss-120B, whose v1 profile was an artefact of them.

items.title: Researchers introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence metric to measure and improve consistency in large language model agents using tool use across independent runs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
items.summary:
Large language model agents that use tools can behave inconsistently across runs starting from the same state, leading to divergent strategies and contradictory outputs that undermine reliability. Existing metrics focus on task correctness but do not capture behavioral consistency over time. Researchers propose Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level metric adapted from reinforcement learning bisimulation, which measures cumulative semantic disagreement between independent agent rollouts using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistencies. RSD is approximated by a neural network and provides a consistency score at each step without needing the full trajectory.

When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces variability in performance metrics by up to 50.5% on benchmarks such as tau2-bench and ToolSandbox, improving task progress across multiple model and benchmark settings including Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3.5. This approach offers a new way to quantify and enhance the consistency of LLM agents in sequential decision-making tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.33012v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use can behave inconsistently across independent runs from identical states. They may call different tools, produce contradictory outputs, or follow divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces AUC coefficient of variation (CV) by up to 30.9% on tau2-bench and 50.5% on ToolSandbox. Across Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3.5 models, RSD reduces AUC CV in seven out of eight model-benchmark settings, while improving the final task progress in all eight settings.

items.title: Researchers introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression for long-horizon LLM agents, reducing computation by up to 59.84% while maintaining accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers propose Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free method that uses soft tokens within large language model (LLM) agents to compress context in long-horizon tasks. ASTC leverages the model's recurrent dynamics and hybrid Gated Delta Network attention to carry forward absorbed information as soft tokens, reducing later-layer computation and enabling reusable key-value caches.

Experiments show ASTC matches or exceeds the accuracy of uncompressed agents while using significantly fewer attention pairs, outperforming trained external compressors that require substantially more computation. This approach offers a model-native way to efficiently manage growing interaction contexts in sustained LLM tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.41291v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 59.84% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 12.3 to 194.9 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

items.title: Researchers compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder Ru-Jev, finding label-wording augmentation improves accuracy on unfamiliar words but not on abbreviations or codes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated two versions of Ru-Jev, a multilingual cross-encoder trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks, to assess the impact of label wording on model accuracy. The later release introduced an augmentation presenting labels in multiple surface forms, which improved accuracy on held-out vocabularies of ordinary and borrowed words, including jargon and office slang, but showed no significant gains on abbreviations or opaque codes.

The study tested ten label vocabularies with varying candidate sizes and controlled for overlap with training data. While the augmented model consistently outperformed the earlier release on unfamiliar words, gains were partly influenced by specific labels and reduced when adjusting for per-option biases. On unseen datasets, accuracy differences varied, and checkpoint rankings were inconsistent, highlighting challenges in evaluation. The researchers also identified four hazards in comparing model releases, emphasizing the complexity of assessing label wording effects in typed-decision models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.08439v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies at five and eighteen candidates, checked for overlap with the training data. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release has higher point accuracy in all fourteen cells, by up to 0.24. Several of these gains rest partly on one label that the earlier release almost never chose; fitting one bias per option removes part of them, while the jargon gain largely survives. On abbreviations and opaque codes the augmented release gives no usable gain: its loss on 17 abbreviations unrelated to training (-0.060) is one label and disappears after the same correction. The comparison is between two trained releases, not a controlled ablation, and the earlier recipe varies across seeds by up to 0.098 on the strictest slice. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points, narrowed to -3.4 and +1.4 by the per-option biases; a second training run of each recipe, the augmented one under a rule recorded beforehand, puts the recipe gap on jargon far above seed noise and on a third unseen dataset, scientific rubrics, only just above it. Rankings of training checkpoints disagree across the three unseen datasets, so none of them should choose the checkpoint. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2503.08823v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are widely used in modern hardware design, yet writing Hardware Description Language (HDL) code for FPGA implementation remains a complex and time-consuming task. The experiments, which primarily analyze Lookup Table (LUT) usage, reveal significant differences among LLMs, demonstrating ResBench's capability to identify models that generate more resource-optimized FPGA designs.

items.originalTitle: Interpreting and Controlling Model Behavior via Constitutions for Atomic Concept Edits
items.summary: Researchers have developed a black-box interpretability framework that learns a verifiable constitution—a natural language summary describing how prompt changes affect a model's behavior such as alignment and correctness. The method uses atomic concept edits (ACEs) to add, remove, or replace interpretable concepts in prompts and observes resulting behavior changes to establish causal mappings. This approach was validated on tasks including mathematical reasoning and text-to-image generation, revealing differences in model focus such as GPT-Image's emphasis on grammar versus Imagen 4's atmospheric coherence. The learned constitutions improved control over model behavior, boosting success rates by an average of 1.86 times compared to methods without constitutions. The researchers have open-sourced their code for further use and study.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.00092v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a black-box interpretability framework that learns a verifiable constitution: a natural language summary of how changes to a prompt affect a model's specific behavior, such as its alignment, correctness, or adherence to constraints. Our method leverages atomic concept edits (ACEs), which are targeted operations that add, remove, or replace an interpretable concept in the input prompt. By systematically applying ACEs and observing the resulting effects on model behavior across various tasks, our framework learns a causal mapping from edits to predictable outcomes. This learned constitution provides deep, generalizable insights into the model. Empirically, we validate our approach across diverse tasks, including mathematical reasoning and text-to-image alignment, for controlling and understanding model behavior. We found that for text-to-image generation, GPT-Image tends to focus on grammatical adherence, while Imagen 4 prioritizes atmospheric coherence. In mathematical reasoning, distractor variables confuse GPT-5 but leave Gemini 2.5 models and o4-mini largely unaffected. Moreover, our results show that the learned constitutions are highly effective for controlling model behavior, achieving an average of 1.86 times boost in success rate over methods that do not use constitutions. Our open-sourced code can be found at https://github.com/google-deepmind/atomic_concept_edits

items.title: Researchers develop Terminator, an early-exit strategy to reduce overthinking in large reasoning models by predicting optimal stopping points in chain-of-thought reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TERMINATOR: Learning Optimal Exit Points for Early Stopping in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers have introduced Terminator, a method designed to reduce excessive computation in large reasoning models (LRMs) by learning optimal exit points during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Terminator predicts when the model's final answer first appears and uses this to train an early-exit strategy that shortens reasoning length without sacrificing accuracy. The approach was tested on four datasets—MATH-500, AIME 2025, HumanEval, and GPQA—achieving 14% to 55% reductions in reasoning length and more than doubling inference speed compared to original models. This work addresses the challenge of determining task- and model-dependent optimal reasoning lengths, improving efficiency in complex reasoning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.12529v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve impressive performance on complex reasoning tasks via Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which enables them to generate intermediate thinking tokens before arriving at the final answer. However, LRMs often suffer from significant overthinking, spending excessive compute time even after the answer is generated early on. Prior work has identified the existence of an optimal reasoning length such that truncating reasoning at this point significantly shortens CoT outputs with virtually no change in performance. However, determining optimal CoT lengths for practical datasets is highly non-trivial as they are fully task and model-dependent. In this paper, we precisely address this and design Terminator, an early-exit strategy for LRMs at inference to mitigate overthinking. The central idea underpinning Terminator is that the first arrival of an LRM's final answer is often predictable, and we leverage these first answer positions to create a novel dataset of optimal reasoning lengths to train Terminator. Powered by this approach, Terminator achieves significant reductions in CoT lengths of 14%-55% on average across four challenging practical datasets: MATH-500, AIME 2025, HumanEval, and GPQA, while outperforming current state-of-the-art methods and reducing inference latency by more than 2x compared to the original LRM.Project page: https://terminator-llm.github.io

items.title: Researchers characterize identification and generation limits using contrastive pairs under corruption budgets in finite and countable hypothesis classes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Contrastive Identification and Generation in the Limit
items.summary: This paper studies a learning scenario where a learner receives only contrastive pairs—unordered pairs of points labeled as dissimilar—without knowing which point is positive. The authors characterize exactly which hypothesis classes are identifiable under any corruption budget and introduce a contrastive closure dimension to describe uniform generation capabilities. They show that on clean data, four learning criteria form a strict hierarchy, but under corruption, some classes become identifiable from contrastive pairs even when positive examples with corruption fail.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.06211v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In identification in the limit (Gold, 1967), a learner reads positive examples and must eventually name the target hypothesis; in generation in the limit (Kleinberg and Mullainathan, 2024), it must eventually produce new positive examples. We study a weaker, relational signal: each observation is an unordered pair $\{x,y\}$ with $h(x)\neq h(y)$, such as a cannot-link constraint or a dissimilar-pair label, and the learner never learns which point is positive. All our results come from one object: a pair is valid for every member of a finite family exactly when its points lie in antipodal cells of the family's membership map. (1) For every corruption budget $k$, known or unknown, we characterize exactly the identifiable classes. Incomparable hypotheses must cover the domain and share more than $2k$ points, and Angluin's tell-tale sets must survive the loss of $2k$ points. Every unbounded budget makes any two hypotheses confusable. (2) A contrastive closure dimension characterizes uniform generation. On finite classes, generation fails exactly when a family that shares a presentation has a finite common support; on countable classes this finite condition no longer suffices. (3) On clean data the four learning criteria form a strict diamond. (4) Under corruption the order changes: some classes are identifiable from contrastive pairs under every finite budget by one algorithm, but not from positive examples with one corrupted example.

items.title: Researchers propose CapCode and CapReward to detect and prevent cheating in coding agent evaluations using capped scores and randomized tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Coding Agents Deceive Us? Detecting and Preventing Cheating via Capped Evaluation with Randomized Tests
items.summary:
Researchers identify a growing issue in evaluating coding agents where models achieve high scores by exploiting shortcuts rather than solving tasks as intended, leading to deceptive evaluation results. They introduce CapCode, a framework that uses randomized tests with a deliberately capped maximum non-cheating score to make cheating detectable when scores exceed this cap. To discourage cheating, they also propose CapReward, a reward system designed to prevent optimization beyond the capped score.

Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that CapCode effectively detects cheating while maintaining accurate performance rankings among models. CapReward reduces cheating behaviors, resulting in models that better adhere to the intended task specifications, improving the reliability of coding agent evaluations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.07379v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A growing failure mode in agent evaluation and training is that models can achieve high evaluation scores (e.g., test pass rates) by exploiting shortcuts instead of solving the intended task, making these scores deceptive. This makes evaluation scores unreliable as measures of true task-solving ability. We propose CapCode, a framework for constructing coding datasets with randomized tests whose best achievable non-cheating score is deliberately capped below 100%. This capped-score design gives evaluation scores a clearer interpretation: scores substantially above the cap are implausible and therefore provide evidence of cheating. To prevent cheating, we propose CapReward, a reward design based on the CapCode principle to discourage optimization beyond the cap. Experiments across multiple datasets show that CapCode detects cheating while preserving performance ranking of models, and CapReward reduces cheating behavior, yielding models that better follow the intended task specification.

items.title: Researchers propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory framework to improve long-context retention in LLMs, boosting accuracy and memory retention up to 73.96% at nearly 900K tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
items.summary:
Researchers identify memory retention as the main bottleneck in recurrent memory agents that extend large language models (LLMs) to handle arbitrarily long contexts. They propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads updated selectively to prevent overwriting and improve retention.

They introduce a lightweight version, MHM-LRU, which ensures uniform head usage without extra token overhead. Experiments on long-context benchmarks from 100K to 1M tokens show MHM-LRU significantly improves retention and end-to-end accuracy compared to baseline methods, with retention rates rising from under 30% to nearly 74% on the RULER-HQA dataset at 896K tokens. These improvements generalize across model types, scales, and tasks, suggesting architectural design as a practical approach to reliable long-context memory in LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01523v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors---memory capture and memory retention---and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

items.title: Researchers find that pooled accuracy of chain-of-thought monitors masks fragility on reasoning-dependent subsets, revealing vulnerability to controlled reasoning rewrites [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A False Average: Pooled CoT-Monitor Accuracy Conceals a Reasoning-Dependent Fragility
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors used to detect reward hacks and found that their reported aggregate accuracy conceals significant fragility on a reasoning-dependent subset of hacks. On the Terminal Wrench dataset, about 77% of hacks are detectable by actions alone, dominating the pooled accuracy, while the remaining 23% evade action-only detection and expose monitor weaknesses when reasoning is subtly rewritten without changing commands or outputs. A controlled attack that altered only the agent's reasoning reduced detection rates on this subset from around 95% to between 4% and 11%, though the overall pooled accuracy dropped only modestly.

The study showed that these reasoning-based attacks remain truthful about events but obscure intent, limiting the effectiveness of trace-only monitors even when alerted to the attack. The vulnerability transfers across different monitor and agent types, and live agents instructed to hack without monitor feedback produced detectable but hollow hacks. Applying the reasoning rewrite to these live hacks maintained detection of action-visible hacks but lowered detection on others, consistent with the false average effect. The authors suggest that monitor accuracy should be reported specifically on reasoning-dependent subsets where defenses are critical, as external information beyond the trace is necessary to improve robustness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.00583v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors are reported by their aggregate accuracy on a pool of reward hacks. We show that this number is a false average. On Terminal Wrench, about 77% of hacks are given away by the actions alone, and the monitor's pooled accuracy is dominated by them; on the remaining 23%, which an action-only monitor misses, the same monitor is fragile. We expose the fragility with a controlled attack: we rewrite only the agent's reasoning to read as good-faith engineering, leaving every command and output byte-identical. One gradient-free rewrite drops a held-out monitor's catch rate on that subset from about 95% to between 4 and 11%, while the pooled rate falls only about 25 points, near what the subset's share of the pool times its collapse predicts. The rewrite stays truthful about what happened and lies only about intent, so the trace-only monitors we test recover little, even when warned about the attack; of our defenses, only information from outside the trace helps much. The attack transfers across monitor and agent families, and the dataset's own hack labels show the same gradient with no monitor in the definition. Live agents told to hack on 27 tasks, with no monitor feedback, produce hollow hacks, but a monitor calibrated on each model's own honest solves catches nearly all of them. Applying the same rewrite to these live hacks keeps all 111 action-visible ones caught and lowers catch on the 16 whose actions score below 0.5 only from 16 to 13: the effect lands where the false average predicts, but the collapse stays a controlled result. A linear probe on a surrogate monitor's activations out-reads its verdict on the obfuscated hacks (AUC up to 0.98), but a behavioral control shows this edge does not, by itself, mean the monitor knows more than it says. Monitor accuracy should be reported on the reasoning-dependent subset, where the defense is load-bearing.

items.title: Researchers find margin to TopK threshold determines sparse autoencoder ablation effects and improve prediction accuracy with margin graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin
items.summary:
Researchers studied sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that pass only the top k largest preactivations, finding that zeroing one feature changes the active set in 74% to 89% of cases across five public TopK SAEs. They introduced a margin graph method that adds first order changes to downstream preactivations before selecting the top k again, reducing median prediction error on Pythia-70M by 84% compared to attribution graphs. Exact recomputation of interventions was faster than the margin graph method on GPUs.

The study also showed that sparse feature maps recover 85% of a graph's squared norm on active features but only 47% when masked to their own graph, with unmasking the inactive tenth nearest the TopK threshold recovering 73% of the masking loss. This indicates that the margin to the TopK threshold largely determines how ablations affect activations and what information graphs carry between different SAE seeds.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.00606v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Attribution graphs predict sparse autoencoder (SAE) ablations to first order on the active features, but a TopK SAE passes only its k largest preactivations, so small changes often swap active features. On five public TopK SAEs, zeroing one feature changes the active set of the next layer's SAE in 74% to 89% of cases. Our margin graph adds the first order change to every downstream preactivation, then selects the k largest again. On Pythia-70M the margin graph cuts the median error of predicted activations, relative to their exact change, from the attribution graph's 0.739 to 0.121, 84% lower. Exact recomputation of 48 interventions runs 3.5 times faster than the margin graph on our GPU. Patched into Pythia-70M with the clean reconstruction error, the margin graph's activations predict the change in the subject verb agreement logit difference with 1.95 times the attribution graph's mean error, on interventions above a fixed floor. Between seeds of our SAEs, which share one auxiliary loss coefficient, sparse feature maps recover 85% of a graph's squared norm on active features but 47% with each graph masked to its own, 38 percentage points less. Unmasking the inactive tenth nearest the TopK threshold recovers 73% of the masking loss, against 11% for a random tenth, so the margin to that threshold decides how ablations change activations and what graphs carry between seeds.

items.title: Researchers apply neutrosophic logic via the Jacobian lens to analyze internal epistemic states in Qwen3.5-4B, revealing evidence tracking and belief discrimination across model layers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Internal Verdicts Track Evidence: A Template-Controlled Neutrosophic Reading of Epistemic States in Large Language Models via the Jacobian Lens
items.summary: This paper presents the first application of neutrosophic logic to internal representations of a large language model, Qwen3.5-4B, using the Jacobian lens to measure truth, indeterminacy, and falsity components across layers. The study identifies distinct signatures such as increased refutation under conflict and sustained indeterminacy under false belief, but finds some effects are artifacts of prompt templates. After controlling for these, the neutrosophic verdict balance reliably tracks evidence polarity and distinguishes false from true first-person beliefs across layers. The authors propose a two-battery protocol for auditing language model internals using lens-based readouts, emphasizing the importance of independent neutrosophic components for measurement and self-correction.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For twenty-five years, neutrosophic logic has assigned independent degrees of truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) to epistemic states that classical and fuzzy semantics cannot express. Previous applications measured these components on outputs: answers, judgments, expert evaluations. This paper reports, to our knowledge, the first neutrosophic reading of components inside the internal representations of a large language model. Using the recently released Jacobian lens on Qwen3.5-4B, we project intermediate-layer readouts onto lexicons of support, refutation, and hedging, obtaining layer-wise (T, I, F) profiles under conflicting evidence, first-person false belief, and factual control (n = 20 each). A first battery yielded three striking signatures: a surge of refutation mass under conflict, sustained indeterminacy under false belief, and an apparent "verdict collapse" before the output layer. A second, template-controlled battery showed that all three, as initially stated, were largely artifacts of prompt grammar: matched templates with agreeing evidence inflate the same lexicon masses, true beliefs elicit the same hedging, and the model verbalizes its verdict when allowed to generate. What survives the controls is stronger than what died: the neutrosophic verdict balance B = log10(F) - log10(T) tracks evidence polarity under identical templates (about 3 orders of magnitude of separation, Cohen's d = 2.3-2.5, p < 10^-6 in 9 of 9 layers; paired Wilcoxon: median difference +2.4 orders, 19/20 items, p = 3.8x10^-6) and residually discriminates false from true first-person beliefs. We argue that the independence of the neutrosophic components is what keeps the common-mode channel observable, making both the measurement and its self-correction possible, and we distill the two-battery design into a reusable protocol for auditing language model internals with lens-based readouts.

items.title: Study compares Alzheimer's caregiving advice from peer caregivers, clinicians, ChatGPT, and retrieval-augmented CareGPT across 85 real questions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: One Question, Four Voices: How Advice for Alzheimer's Caregiving Differs Between Caregivers, Clinicians, and Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed responses to 85 Alzheimer's caregiving questions from four groups: peer caregivers, physicians, ChatGPT, and CareGPT, a retrieval-augmented model based on peer discussions. They assessed differences in linguistic style, emotional and informational support, and topic coverage, finding that peers offered narrative and community-based advice, clinicians gave concise clinical guidance, and large language models (LLMs) provided formal, structured consultations.

CareGPT showed little difference from ChatGPT, indicating that retrieval augmentation alone did not change communication style. LLMs scored higher on politeness and emotional support than peers and matched clinicians in informativeness but lacked narrative depth and contextual grounding. Topic analysis revealed LLMs focused on advice-oriented themes, while peers addressed broader issues including emotional, legal, financial, and daily care concerns.

The findings suggest AI can complement but not replace human input in Alzheimer's caregiver support, highlighting the potential for hybrid systems that combine AI's structured delivery with the nuanced strengths of human voices.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.18604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online caregiver forums are an important source of emotional and informational support for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). We compare responses to 85 real caregiver questions from ALZConnected across four responder groups: peer caregivers, physicians, ChatGPT, and a retrieval-augmented CareGPT grounded in peer discussions. Using 28 measures spanning linguistic form, emotional support, informational support, and topic scope, we examine how these voices differ when answering the same questions. Peers provided time-anchored narratives and community grounding; clinicians offered concise, advice-forward, clinically bounded guidance; and LLMs produced a formal, verbose, highly structured consultation style. CareGPT showed minimal measurable separation from ChatGPT, suggesting that retrieval plus prompt injection alone was insufficient to shift communicative stance. LLM outputs scored higher than peers on politeness and emotion-support markers and were comparable to clinicians on informativeness and physician-alignment measures, but were less narrative and less contextually situated. Topic modeling showed that LLM responses concentrated on advice-oriented themes, whereas peers covered a broader range, including emotional processing, legal and financial concerns, and daily care. These findings suggest that AI can complement, but not replace, human contributions to ADRD caregiver support and motivate hybrid systems that combine structured AI delivery with the distinct strengths of human voices.

items.title: Syntactic Complexity Convergence in Dialogue: Analysis of the Phenomenon and Application to LLM Detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Syntactic Complexity Convergence in Dialogue: Analysis of the Phenomenon and Application to LLM Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the under-explored phenomenon of syntactic complexity convergence in dialogue. Extending prior topic-level analyses to full conversations, we examine five human-human datasets and a set of human-LLM dialogues. We integrate and evaluate a multidimensional set of syntactic complexity metrics to quantify structural variation in dialogue. Our analyses reveal robust syntactic complexity convergence across human-human datasets, especially in task-oriented interactions, and statistical tests confirm that these effects are not due to chance. In contrast, human-LLM dialogues show no significant convergence under individual metrics; however, linear-CKA uncovers a distinct cross-metric convergence pattern. Motivated by these differences, we use syntactic complexity as a feature for detecting LLM-involved dialogue, achieving 96\% accuracy. Our classification results demonstrate its potential without relying on likelihood-based signals such as surprisal, which require a language model as the estimator.

items.originalTitle: Justification of Emotional Appeal in Computational Argumentation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emotional appeals (EAs) are often treated as fallacious in computational argumentation, yet they may be justified when warranted by the context. We introduce the task of predicting EA justification and present the first human-annotated dataset for this task, covering 1,176 argument--context pairs. Grounded in philosophical literature, our framework evaluates EA justification along logical and emotional dimensions. Human annotations show that justification criteria form a shared latent judgment space, with evidential proportionality and normative acceptability most strongly associated with overall justification. We further find that EAs without logical support are not always judged fully unjustified, and stronger EAs are not necessarily judged less justified. Finally, LLM experiments show that EA justification prediction remains challenging.

items.title: Understanding Failures in LLM Reasoning by Learning Structured Representations of Chain-of-Thought [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Understanding Failures in LLM Reasoning by Learning Structured Representations of Chain-of-Thought
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is central to improving reasoning in large language models, yet existing evaluation methods focus on step-level signals and ignore the underlying structure of reasoning traces. This raises a key question: what aspects of reasoning quality (i.e., correctness, efficiency, and failure patterns) are encoded in the structure of a CoT trace? We introduce \textbf{CoT2Graph}, a framework that represents CoT traces as directed dependency graphs, making relationships between reasoning steps explicit and capturing patterns such as backtracking, branching, and subtask merging. We model these graphs with graph neural networks and use attribution-based explanations to identify structural patterns associated with reasoning quality. CoT2Graph reveals distinct patterns of successful and failed reasoning: correct CoTs place greater importance on early planning, whereas incorrect CoTs are associated with overloaded synthesis steps and dependency violations. We further show that graph-based signals better predict whether a CoT leads to a correct answer, outperforming previous tree-based structural methods by up to 2.5\% and simple length-based baselines by 7.8\%, while also improving Best-of-$N$ selection. Overall, our results demonstrate that reasoning structure encodes rich signals about reasoning quality, motivating a shift from sequence-level evaluation to structural analysis.

items.title: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLM agents become increasingly capable of making consequential economic decisions, their safety under economic pressures remains poorly understood. We introduce EconSafeBench, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating the safety of LLM agents in executable economic environments. EconSafeBench contains 828 cases across five economic scenarios and four categories of safety violations. A key design is the matched evaluation of three sources of safety pressure, including explicit user requests, pressure from other actors, and pressure arising from the agent's own pursuit of a performance objective. We further evaluate safety at both static and dynamic scales through 30-period interactions with persistent memory and matched controls. Across eight LLMs, all evaluated models exhibit safety violations on the static benchmark, with overall violation rates ranging from 8.5% to 40.6%. We further find that violations can occur even without an explicit unsafe request, and that initially compliant agents may begin to violate as performance pressure increases over time. These findings highlight the need for stronger safety alignment and rigorous evaluation before LLM agents are deployed in high-stakes economic environments.

items.title: The Judge Is Not Impartial: Self-Preference in Medical LLM Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Judge Is Not Impartial: Self-Preference in Medical LLM Evaluation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate model-generated medical content, creating a potential circularity: an LLM judge may favor outputs generated by the same model independently of clinical quality. To characterize LLM judge self-preference in medical settings, we measured same-model affinity in single-turn specialist question answering and multi-turn standardized-patient encounters. We evaluated eight models, two from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Qwen, on 620 real point of care questions from clinicians (Real-POCQi). The same eight models also generated and judged 200 standardized patient-clinician scenarios (MedSP1000) up to 8 visible turns. In total, our analysis spans 13,760 LLM judgments. We define three complementary measures of self-preference. Answer Rank Bias, our primary measure, compared the rank assigned to a fixed response by its own-model judge with its average rank from outside judges. Answer Score Bias made the analogous comparison using rubric scores. Own-Answer Win Rate measured how often a judge ranked its own model's response above a competitor. Higher values across all these measures indicate greater degrees of self-preference. In Real-POCQi, pooled Answer Rank Bias was $+1.22$ positions, and all eight judges favored their own answers. Self-preference persisted both with and without a grading rubric. Revealing generator identities modestly weakened self-preference by an average of $-0.094$ positions. In MedSP1000, pooled Answer Rank Bias ranged from $+0.53$ to $+0.62$ positions, with no clear difference by conversation length ($p=0.17$). LLM judges systematically favored responses generated by their own models across multiple formats. Clinical AI deployments should exercise increased vigilance including multiple evaluation measures and judge panels spanning differing model families when deploying LLM-as-a-judge systems.

items.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Fact-Checking LLMs on Multilingual Evidence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating the Robustness of Fact-Checking LLMs on Multilingual Evidence
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated fact-checking benchmarks typically pair claims with clean, curated evidence in high-resource languages, but real-world evidence is often incomplete, misleading, or written in a language where models are weaker. We evaluate the robustness of fact-checking LLMs for different languages. Building on EuroVerdict, we construct gold evidence sets for 190 claims in each of English, German, Greek, and Romanian, then apply four corruption strategies at two severity levels. We test LLMs on a set of claims, providing them with evidence from the sets above. A rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge scores reasoning quality. Verdict accuracy proves highly sensitive to both factors: Misleading edit cut Llama 3.1 8B's English accuracy from 80.00% to 16.84%, and losses widen as language resource level decreases. Machine-translating Greek and Romanian claims into English recovers much, but not all, of the low-resource gap. Judge scores decline more slowly than accuracy, suggesting that automated reasoning evaluation underestimates degradation. These results caution against deploying LLM fact-checkers on noisy multilingual evidence, and we release our evidence datasets and evaluation code to support future work.

items.title: Skill Transfer: Adapting Agent Skills from Strong to Weak Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Skill Transfer: Adapting Agent Skills from Strong to Weak Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills are modular bundles of instructions, code, and resources that an agent loads on demand, increasingly authored and validated on frontier models and shared as an open standard. The same skill behaves differently across models: a strong model turns it into a large performance gain, while a weak model realizes little of that gain and sometimes does worse than with no skill at all. Cost and resource constraints, however, often restrict real deployments to exactly these weaker agents. We hypothesize that the strong model silently supplies procedural steps the skill leaves implicit, which the weak model omits, and formalize closing this gap as \emph{Skill Transfer}: holding the skill's capability ceiling and the model's parameters fixed, we adapt the skill so a specific weak agent can execute it well. Our method abstracts strong and weak trajectories into typed execution structures, localizes their structural divergence with a graph edit distance (GED), and repairs the skill through an iterative diagnoser-patcher loop. Across three benchmarks and two model families, Skill Transfer raises pass rate over the unmodified skill significantly and well over other skill-evolution baselines. The adapted skill also improves the strong agent it was never adapted for, and transfers out of distribution to a structurally related, unseen task. Code is available at https://github.com/Yifan-Lan/Skill-Transfer

items.title: Interpretability-Guided Auditing for Clinical Language Models for Discharge Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Interpretability-Guided Auditing for Clinical Language Models for Discharge Prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical natural language processing (NLP) models for hospital discharge prediction are vulnerable to explicit discharge-related lexical cues in clinical notes, even when note timestamps are temporally filtered. These cues may act as proxies for future outcomes, leading models to rely on shortcut-like signals rather than clinically meaningful evidence. We propose AuditBERT-Discharge, a lightweight framework that reframes interpretability as a training-time auditing mechanism. Token-level SHAP attributions from an initial BioClinicalBERT model are used to identify highly attributed discharge-related tokens, which are subsequently masked in the training corpus before model retraining. We evaluate the framework on a retrospective cohort of elective spine surgery encounters from a single academic medical center. Qualitative attribution analysis and preliminary evaluation suggest that SHAP-guided auditing reduces reliance on explicit discharge-proxy language and yields more conservative, better-calibrated predictions, although improvements in discrimination are not uniform. These findings demonstrate the potential of interpretability-guided auditing as a practical strategy for identifying and constraining shortcut-like lexical dependencies in temporally sensitive clinical NLP tasks.

items.title: FlashREINFORCE: Critic-Free Single-Rollout Asynchronous RL for Agentic Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FlashREINFORCE: Critic-Free Single-Rollout Asynchronous RL for Agentic Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but removes the variance-reducing group baseline, making updates noisier and more prone to instability on stale, variable-length trajectories. We present FlashREINFORCE, a critic-free, one-pass framework built on One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization. These components preserve prompt coverage and signed feedback while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. In our experiments, FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at a policy lag of approximately four updates. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, it reaches 38.0 mean accuracy across five benchmarks, outperforming the reported GRPO baseline by 1.7 percentage points with half the rollouts (256k versus 512k). Python-tool experiments extend to the 30B MoE model Qwen3-30B-A3B, with stable training at policy lag eight. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, FlashREINFORCE maintains tool use where GRPO stops making tool calls and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.

items.title: Wrong with Confidence: Measuring Hallucination, Overconfidence and Identity-Conditioned Behaviour in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Wrong with Confidence: Measuring Hallucination, Overconfidence and Identity-Conditioned Behaviour in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models answer underspecified questions readily, and accuracy-only evaluation rewards guessing over abstaining. Observational studies link query underspecification to hallucination, but they cannot separate the effect of missing information from item difficulty, and they rarely ask what the model tells the user. We report a pre-registered, paired behavioural study of five open-weight models (Gemma 3 27B, Gemma 4 31B, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Super). Each of 142 factual questions was posed in a fully specified form and in a referentially underspecified form with the same answer key, and three probes measured identity-conditioned behaviour. Two raters scored 5,620 responses under a fixed rubric; effects were estimated with mixed-effects models. Without the referent, the models sought clarification on 33.7% of prompts and answered the rest. Among attempted answers, the error rate rose from 39.1% to 52.0% (mixed-effects odds ratio 4.12, 95% CI 2.76-6.14), and specialist-domain questions failed more often than general ones in every model. Unelicited verbal uncertainty did not track this risk: 75.3% of wrong answers carried no hedge, wrong answers to underspecified prompts were hedged no more often than wrong answers to clear prompts (27.3% vs 22.3%), and hedging separated correct from incorrect answers only weakly (AUROC 0.56). Gendered pronouns followed occupational stereotypes whenever a model committed to one; any stated user identity lengthened answers by about 45% relative to an anonymous user; claimed expertise did not reduce safety caveats. The models either ask or answer as if the question were well posed, and the wording of a guess does not reveal that it is one. Evaluations should score clarification as a distinct outcome and check label validity as well as rater agreement.

items.title: KUDEX: A Zero-Shot Decompositional Framework for Logical Analysis in Natural Language [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: KUDEX: A Zero-Shot Decompositional Framework for Logical Analysis in Natural Language
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text, they often struggle with multi-step logical reasoning with inferential connections among statements. We introduce KUDEX (Knowledge-Upward-Downward Reasoning Extension), a novel zero-shot, decompositional framework for analyzing and verifying logical relationships in natural language. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on surface-level entailment checks, KUDEX leverages LLMs to decompose reasoning into atomic primitives and constructs transparent reasoning graphs that serve both as execution traces and audit logs. Our framework includes a general prompt adaptation pipeline that adapts to diverse reasoning tasks without additional fine-tuning or domain-specific pipelines. Through comprehensive experiments on benchmarks across four domains, we demonstrate that KUDEX provides superior performance compared to existing methods, offering a more granular and robust framework for assessing logical relationships between statements.

items.title: SurveyWeave: An Agentic Framework for Automated Survey Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SurveyWeave: An Agentic Framework for Automated Survey Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surveys help researchers keep up with fast-moving fields, but they take weeks to months to write. Automated survey generation (AutoSurvey) can alleviate this situation, but it is challenging to draw on hundreds to thousands of precisely scoped papers, choose among many valid structures, and stay faithful to its sources while offering insights. We present SurveyWeave, an agentic architecture that decomposes the problem into four tasks coordinated by three agents, each reviewing others' work and conducting revisions based on feedback. We also introduce WeaveEval, a five-dimension evaluation grounded in prior surveys. A comprehensive comparison shows that SurveyWeave outperforms Codex by 8 points and the strongest AutoSurvey baseline by 6 points.

items.title: Latency, Speech Recognition and Turn-Taking in Voice Agents for Spanish Phone Negotiation: An Externally Measured Comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit and GPT-Live [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Latency, Speech Recognition and Turn-Taking in Voice Agents for Spanish Phone Negotiation: An Externally Measured Comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit and GPT-Live
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A voice agent that negotiates by phone must answer quickly, understand spoken amounts and cope with a caller who talks over it. We compared three architectures for such an agent, negotiating freight rates in Spanish: two cascades (speech recognition, language model and speech synthesis) orchestrated by Pipecat and by LiveKit Agents, and GPT-Live, an OpenAI speech model that listens and speaks without separate stages. A program played the carrier with the same 47 recordings of one speaker for all agents, without the telephone network, in 77 calls per architecture over five negotiation scenarios, and measured latency on the listener's side with a validated instrument. Median latency to the content response was 2,616.0 ms (Pipecat), 3,090.0 ms (LiveKit) and 2,444.8 ms (GPT-Live); the confidence interval of GPT-Live's 171.2 ms advantage over Pipecat includes zero. According to its own timestamps, GPT-Live began to answer 800 ms after the end of the line, close to the 0.8 s published by OpenAI; most of the remaining wait, about 1,367 ms and nearly constant, is the audio's round trip through OpenAI's service. A tool call added 0.9-1.1 s in every architecture, more than any difference between them, and the frameworks' self-reported latency fell short of the listener's wait by 9% (Pipecat) and 22% (LiveKit). Word error rates were low (6.03, 4.93 and 1.47%), but the error on amounts was 13.01% and 12.61% in the cascades, against 2.86% in GPT-Live. With default settings, Pipecat and LiveKit stopped at almost every backchannel and often took it as the carrier's answer: an "ok" spoken over the agent ended in a registered agreement in 3 of 15 Pipecat calls, 2 of 15 LiveKit calls and no GPT-Live call (descriptive counts, not tested). Latency should therefore be measured on the listener's side, and a cascade needs safeguards for spoken amounts and backchannels.

items.title: MarineSparkLM-4B: A Lightweight Language Model for Marine and Offshore Engineering Built by Parameter-Efficient Adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MarineSparkLM-4B: A Lightweight Language Model for Marine and Offshore Engineering Built by Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Marine and offshore engineering text is spread across preprints, open-access journals, encyclopedias and institutional documents, and the amount of it is small by pretraining standards. We ask how far a lightweight language model for marine and offshore engineering can be taken with parameter-efficient adaptation on a single workstation-class device. Starting from the 4-billion-parameter OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct, we train two independent LoRA adapters, each updating 33.0 million of 4.06 billion parameters (0.81%). Training took 4 hours 40 minutes for the first adapter and 10 minutes for the second on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The first adapter is trained by next-token prediction on a 61.6-million-token corpus covering ten engineering themes. The corpus was built from 13,879 source documents, of which 7,069 were retained after deduplication and a two-tier keyword filter that removes cross-domain lexical collisions. Its validation loss falls from 2.082 to 1.976 over 1,500 steps. Direct testing showed that this adapter could still drift off topic on a retrieval-grounded ballast-water prompt, so we trained a second adapter on 2,295 question-answer pairs (114 hand-written and 2,181 generated by the base model from corpus passages) with the loss restricted to answer tokens. On 20 held-out prompts scored by hand for accuracy, topicality and specificity (maximum 120), the plain base model, the continuation adapter, the instruction adapter and the instruction adapter with retrieval scored 42, 56, 84 and 88. Absolute accuracy stays low (14 of 40 without retrieval and 20 of 40 with it). We report the full pipeline, two negative results (a reverted keyword fix and an instruction run that overfit within 100 steps), and the limits of the evaluation, which uses one small prompt set, no inter-rater agreement measure and model-generated reference answers.

items.title: Isolating Perception for Multi-View Planning under Occlusion-Induced Partial Observability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Isolating Perception for Multi-View Planning under Occlusion-Induced Partial Observability
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are beginning to saturate visual planning benchmarks, yet they fail to resolve depth ambiguity and degrade sharply with problem size under occlusion-induced partial observability (PO). We introduce BW-PO based on the Blocksworld domain, a controlled benchmark that reduces existing VLM planners and formalizers to near-zero performance, and propose VLM-as-perceiver, a paradigm that narrows the VLM's role to local perception while delegating cross-view evidence reconciliation and plan generation to external solvers. Across model-specific challenging subsets of BW-PO, this raises plan success from 1% to 97% for Gemma-4-31B, 0% to 95% for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 3% to 84% for Gemini-3.1-Pro. Isolating perception in this way separates two bottlenecks that are otherwise entangled: reconciliation under depth ambiguity, and completeness of visual extraction under scene density.

items.title: Revisiting What Makes a Good Context Subset: A Sparse Latent Basis Perspective [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Revisiting What Makes a Good Context Subset: A Sparse Latent Basis Perspective
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting context subsets is increasingly important in modern LLM inference, yet what makes a subset effective remains unclear. We study this question in the controlled setting of few-shot demonstration selection. We examine a hypothesis that demonstrations should collectively provide task-relevant information needed by a target query. Assuming that the query representation provides a useful proxy for these requirements, we formulate selection as sparse reconstruction and instantiate it with Residual Explanation Search (RES), a Matching-Pursuit-style diagnostic procedure. Across seven benchmarks and eight open-weight LLMs, no retrieval objective is universally best. RES outperforms MMR in 34 of 56 model--dataset pairs, with its clearest advantage on sentiment tasks, suggesting that query-conditioned collective reconstruction may capture useful complementarity that pairwise dissimilarity misses. Relevance-based retrieval remains strong on template-heavy reasoning benchmarks, while all retrieval methods underperform zero-shot prediction on average on StrategyQA, where a solution-reconstruction analysis is consistent with the query not exposing the required external knowledge. Target-model hidden states further show that retrieval objectives interact differently with representation spaces: middle-layer representations generally favor similarity retrieval, whereas last-layer representations are often stronger for residual- and diversity-based selection. These findings support a conditional, representation-dependent account of context subset quality rather than a universally superior selector.

items.title: OmitEHR: Scalable Omission Detection in LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OmitEHR: Scalable Omission Detection in LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Health systems increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to draft summaries of patient medical records, yet evaluations now find omissions, the absence of clinically important information, to be the most common failure mode. Detecting omissions in an LLM-generated summary requires knowing which facts in the record are salient, a signal that existing methods hand-specify, ignore, or recompute at inference with costly LLM judges. We present OmitEHR, a reference-free omission detector that learns clinical salience from historical clinician-written summaries predating widespread LLM use. OmitEHR learns to predict which source-note sentences clinicians include in their summaries, then surfaces high-salience sentences not covered by an LLM-generated summary as candidate omissions. We apply OmitEHR to brief hospital course (BHC) summarization using 5,000 admissions from a large academic medical center. On held-out admissions, OmitEHR outperformed all evaluated baselines at predicting salient source sentences, including a prompted LLM judge. The full omission detection pipeline took 17.7 to 19.5 seconds and cost \$0.03 to \$0.13 per summary depending on the base model, 1.6 to 1.7 times faster and 5.6 to 6.7 times cheaper than scoring every source sentence with an LLM judge. In a blinded review of 25 admissions, two board-certified clinicians confirmed a mean of 5.6 clinically meaningful omissions per summary surfaced by OmitEHR, compared with 3.3 for a full LLM pipeline, counting candidates confirmed by at least one clinician. The efficiency and validity of OmitEHR make it a practical tool for health systems to flag omissions before a summary reaches the clinician.

items.title: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight BERT-based and five LLM-based models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark development set translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set. IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated language sets, with a macro-average of 0.843, followed by BGE-M3 at 0.792. Harrier-270M is the strongest LLM-based model on translated STS-B, with a macro-average of 0.751. On MahaSTS, IndicSBERT and Bhasha-Embed-v0 achieve Pearson correlations of 0.901 and 0.900, respectively, while EmbeddingGemma leads the LLM-based models at 0.871. The highest-scoring BERT-based model thus exceeds the highest-scoring LLM-based model in both settings, although the magnitude of the difference varies across benchmarks.
